content: 1. Health is defined as a state of complete physical, mental, and social well-being, not merely the absence of disease or infirmity. It is recognized as a fundamental human right, and achieving the highest possible level of health is considered a critical global social goal. This goal requires coordinated actions across various social and economic sectors, in addition to the health sector. 2. The significant disparities in health status between developed and developing countries, as well as within individual nations, are politically, socially, and economically unacceptable. These inequalities are a matter of shared concern for all countries. 3. Economic and social development, guided by a New International Economic Order, is essential for achieving the highest attainable health standards for all. It also plays a crucial role in narrowing the health gap between developed and developing nations. Promoting and protecting public health is vital for sustained economic and social progress, contributing to improved quality of life and global peace. 4. Individuals have both the right and the responsibility to actively participate, both individually and collectively, in the planning and implementation of their healthcare. 5. Governments bear the responsibility for the health of their populations. This obligation can only be fulfilled through the provision of adequate health and social measures. A primary social objective for governments, international organizations, and the global community should be to ensure that by the year 2000, all people achieve a level of health that enables them to lead socially and economically productive lives. Primary healthcare is the cornerstone for achieving this target, as it aligns with the principles of social justice. 6. Primary healthcare is defined as essential healthcare that is practical, scientifically sound, and socially acceptable. It must be universally accessible to individuals and families in the community, with their full participation, and at a cost that the community and country can sustain at every stage of development. This approach emphasizes self-reliance and self-determination. Primary healthcare is central to a country’s health system and is integral to the overall social and economic development of the community. It represents the first level of contact between individuals, families, and the national health system, bringing healthcare as close as possible to where people live and work. It also serves as the initial element in a continuous healthcare process. 7. Primary healthcare evolves from the economic, sociocultural, and political characteristics of a country and its communities. It is based on the application of relevant findings from social, biomedical, and public health research. It addresses the primary health issues in the community by providing promotive, preventive, curative, and rehabilitative services. It includes essential components such as health education, proper nutrition, safe water supply, basic sanitation, maternal and child healthcare, immunization, disease prevention, appropriate treatment of common illnesses and injuries, and access to essential medicines. It involves collaboration across various sectors, including agriculture, education, housing, and public works, requiring coordinated efforts. It promotes community and individual self-reliance and participation in healthcare planning and implementation. It is supported by integrated and functional referral systems, prioritizing those most in need. It relies on trained health workers, including physicians, nurses, midwives, and community health workers, to respond effectively to the community’s health needs. 8. Governments should develop national policies, strategies, and action plans to implement and sustain primary healthcare as part of a comprehensive national health system. This requires political will, mobilization of resources, and rational use of external resources. 9. Countries should cooperate in a spirit of partnership to ensure primary healthcare for all, recognizing that health improvements in one country benefit others. The joint WHO/UNICEF report on primary healthcare provides a solid foundation for further development and implementation worldwide. 10. Achieving an acceptable level of health for all by the year 2000 is possible through better utilization of global resources, including reallocating funds currently spent on armaments and military conflicts. A genuine policy of peace and disarmament could release additional resources for social and economic development, with primary healthcare receiving its fair share. 11. The International Conference on Primary Healthcare calls for urgent and effective national and international actions to develop and implement primary healthcare globally, particularly in developing countries. It urges governments, WHO, UNICEF, international organizations, and funding agencies to support primary healthcare initiatives and provide increased technical and financial assistance, especially in developing nations. 12. The conference emphasizes the need for collaboration among all stakeholders to introduce, develop, and sustain primary healthcare in line with the principles outlined in this declaration. It reaffirms the values of equity, solidarity, social justice, universal access, and community participation as the foundation for strengthening health systems. 13. Member States are urged to ensure political commitment to the principles of the Alma-Ata Declaration, prioritize health system strengthening, and accelerate progress toward universal access to primary healthcare. This includes developing equitable and sustainable financing mechanisms, integrating palliative care, and ensuring comprehensive service delivery models. 14. Governments are encouraged to train and retain adequate numbers of health workers with appropriate skills, integrate disease-specific programs into primary healthcare, improve access to essential medicines and technologies, and strengthen health information systems to support evidence-based policies. 15. The WHO Director-General is requested to ensure that the organization’s efforts align with the Alma-Ata Declaration’s principles, support Member States in strengthening primary healthcare, and facilitate the exchange of experiences and best practices. WHO should also coordinate global health interventions and ensure adequate funding for health system strengthening and primary healthcare revitalization.
